top3.why: PhilaMOCA screens Dust Devil, Richard Stanley's near-mythic 1992 desert horror about a shapeshifting serial killer stalking the South African wasteland — a film that spent decades in butchered cuts before its restoration made repertory bookings like this one possible. It's the kind of genre deep-cut that made PhilaMOCA's reputation, projected in a former mausoleum showroom instead of a multiplex. Doors 7:00 PM, film at 7:30 PM; $10.

The Little Haiti Chapter hosts a community causerie on immigration and affordable housing, bringing residents, advocates, and local leaders together to compare notes on two of the crises hitting Philadelphia's immigrant communities hardest right now. It's a working conversation rather than a rally — small, substantive, and easy to miss if you're not already plugged into the group. Free.

Shaun Milli brings a soul voice with more depth than his age suggests to City Winery, ahead of a new album he's readying for 2026. He's framed his own project as a throughline to the soul and R&B artists who came before him — a nod worth taking seriously in a city with Philadelphia International Records in its bones. Table service available; note the venue's dinner-show format if you just want the music.

top3.why: Esperanza Spalding — bassist, vocalist, and one of the defining jazz artists of her generation — plays an intimate three-piece set drawing from all eight of her albums plus a preview of new material. It's a rare small-room booking for an artist who usually fills much bigger stages, and 100% of proceeds go to PRISMID Sanctuary, an Indigenous- and Black-led eco-cultural nonprofit. Second and final night of a two-night run (also Aug 26).

A discussion group on Bayard Rustin's overlooked "Freedom Budget for All Americans" — the jobs-centric economic vision from the organizer who built the March on Washington but rarely gets credit for the ideas behind it. Led by Paul Prescod, it's political education in the literal sense: reading and arguing through an alternative to austerity politics, not just another lecture. Free, Rittenhouse Square.

Cursor Philly marks one year since its first meetup with an anniversary gathering at Indy Hall — from a small room talking about a new AI coding tool to one of the city's more active tech communities. Worth catching for the retrospective angle as much as the usual demos and networking. Northern Liberties: nearest stop is the Market-Frankford Line at Girard Ave, about a half-mile walk.

top3.why: A stacked four-band DIY bill of grindcore, powerviolence, and death metal touches down at Cousin Danny's — Voidhammer down from LA, Harsh Realm from Asheville, plus locals Diuretic and Agonesiac. This is the unfiltered end of the punk/hardcore spectrum: no ticketing platform, no venue website, just a house-show-adjacent DIY space and a wall of noise. West Philadelphia past University City — nearest stop is 46th St on the Market-Frankford Line.

The Philadelphia Film Society continues its Dekalog Special Series with parts 5 and 6 of Kieślowski's ten-part meditation on the Ten Commandments, screening in 4K — a defense attorney's crisis of conscience over a death-penalty case, paired with a teenager's obsessive fixation on his neighbor. Widely regarded as one of the towering achievements in film history, and a rare chance to see it as intended: on a big screen, in installments. Likely at PFS Film Society Center, based on the day's other PFS repertory booking.

Philly DSA canvasses Kingsessing for Chris Rabb, a democratic socialist running for PA-03 on universal healthcare, childcare, and abolishing ICE — retail politics for a candidate trying to prove a socialist can actually win a Philadelphia congressional seat. No experience needed; new canvassers are paired with a partner, and there's a debrief after. Kingsessing, Southwest Philadelphia — bus-served (routes 17/64), no nearby rail station.

top3.why: Collide Zine presents "Self Creation, Surplus Imagination" with Stealing Time at Wooden Shoe Books — an anti-capitalist meditation on reclaiming time and imagination from wage work, in zine and discussion form. It's the anarchist bookstore's whole reason for being: political theory that isn't academic, delivered somewhere you can actually talk back. Free, South Street.

Evil Pony Productions stages a burlesque tribute to punk music and culture, Riot Grrrl chapter — "Girls to the Front" made literal. It's a different register than a straight band show, but the same underlying culture: DIY, feminist, and built around a scene rather than a headliner. Northern Liberties — nearest stop is Girard on the Market-Frankford Line. $15.71-$23.18.

Untitled Medical Collective and Philly SRA teach Bleeding Control Basics at Iffy Books — scene safety, injury assessment, and tourniquet application, the kind of street-medic skills mutual aid networks actually train on. No certification, just information they want as many people as possible to have. Face masks required.

top3.why: The Palestinian Feminist Collective and Progressive International launch "A Predatory State," a 200-page report documenting Israeli sexualized and gendered violence against Palestinians, with a panel featuring Palestinian legal scholar and human rights attorney Noura Erakat. This is a rare chance to hear a leading legal voice on the topic in person rather than through a clip online. Free, RSVP via Action Network. *(confirm exact venue address)*

Kiyoshi Kurosawa's Cure (1997) closes out PFS's Terror Trilogy series in 4K — a detective drawn into a string of murders committed by seemingly ordinary people under a stranger's hypnotic influence. Kurosawa built his reputation turning modern Japan into a landscape of quiet dread, and this is the film critics point to first. Likely at PFS Film Society Center, based on other bookings under this venue listing.

Build a fully offline GPS unit at Iffy Books — a Pi Pico microcontroller, a GPS module, and a tiny OLED display, wired up in MicroPython to show your coordinates and the time with no internet or cell connection at all. It's DIY electronics at its most quietly radical: a gadget that works precisely because it can't be tracked, monetized, or bricked by a company's server going dark. Requires a ~$40-50 parts kit, purchased separately.

top3.why: Wooden Shoe Books hosts an initial interest meeting for a prisoner-correspondence penpal program serving LGBTQIA+ people currently incarcerated. No commitment required to attend — organizers will explain how the program works, and there's an option to write one-time letters to specific political prisoners if a long-term penpal relationship isn't feasible. Quiet, unglamorous solidarity work of exactly the kind that's easy to walk past.

A five-band crust/hardcore punk bill headlined by out-of-towners Pray to Be Saved, with locals Sediment, Ln Celestine, Insectoids, and Dystrophy filling out the night. No ticketing platform, no venue website — just a DIY show flyer and a scene that runs on word of mouth. *(confirm venue address before attending)*

TEASE returns to Club 624 for its second pop-up, produced with NIGHTBLOOM — a collective of dancers with experience in Philly's strip clubs building something safer and more affirming than the standard club circuit. The night centers Black lesbian, queer, and trans people specifically, and this summer's run is fundraising for organizations supporting Black trans people. Community-run nightlife, not a branded night out.

top3.why: Froggy — a Philly queer punk power trio who started as teenagers in 2020 — headline with New York's PLEASURE DEATH, a queer heavy-grunge duo, and The Angies. Froggy write punchy, melodic songs about the mundane and absurd parts of growing up (711 nachos gets a shoutout), channeling L7, Bikini Kill, and The Dead Milkmen without imitating them. Fishtown — nearest stop is Berks or Girard on the Market-Frankford Line.

Scribe Video Center's community-powered Street Movies! joins forces with Black Earth Urban Ag Hub's new documentary series for a screening on urban agriculture, Black agrarian futures, and Philadelphia's legacies of land-based resilience. It's participatory by design — film, conversation, and collective reflection about who gets to shape the city's food systems, not a passive sit-and-watch. *(confirm exact venue location)*

Eastern State Penitentiary's monthly ASL-interpreted guide-led tour pairs the site's history with a direct conversation about the role of prisons in society today — full ASL and voice interpretation, welcoming D/deaf, hard-of-hearing, and hearing visitors alike. A rare instance of an already-thoughtful historic-site tour built for genuine accessibility from the ground up. Fairmount — reachable via SEPTA bus (routes 7/32/48), roughly a 15-20 minute walk from the Spring Garden stop on the Broad Street Line.
